rationale: The original body and separate table of contents each contain 237 visible numbered entries, 216 with abstracts and 21 withdrawn. Members 125 and 162 report dribbling and salivation measures across genetic or motor subtype comparisons. Member 70 only cites a separate saliva paper. No member pairs raw fig with graded drooling.
A Parkinson functional scale was adapted for PKAN. Its distinct salivation item was understood by 38 of 39. This is instrument validation in a different disease without an ingredient comparison.
The brainstem review discusses possible vagal and catecholamine contributions to salivation alongside dysphagia. It provides no measured food contrast or raw-fig estimate.
The clinical teaching article discusses drooling among features of a different diagnosis. It supplies neither a Parkinson population contrast nor a culinary intervention.
The Alzheimer-model study mentions Parkinson drooling in background text. Its experimental outcomes concern constipation. It measures no Parkinson drooling or raw fig.

The article has original support-group and interview material. One patient links food spills and drooling to avoidance of public settings. It does not name a causal food or grade change after raw fig.
The review cites Mao for a sex and subtype difference in drooling. It does not report a separate food comparison or new patient-level estimate.

The nutrition and microbiota review lists drooling among Parkinson gastrointestinal symptoms. The intervention examples address microbiota, bowel, metabolic or broader Parkinson outcomes. No reported raw-fig or separate drooling comparison.
The drug-repurposing analysis retrieves salivation indications in compound tables. It is not a patient dietary experiment or new drooling outcome study.
A clinical review of dystonia and tics mentions sialorrhea in treatment indication listings. Its source neither tests raw fig nor reports a Parkinson food-related symptom estimate.
